title: He Spent 30 Seconds Inside a Whale's Mouth #shorts
description:
Case 004. 11 June 2021, off Provincetown, Cape Cod: lobster diver Michael Packard, 56, was about 45 feet down when a humpback whale closed its mouth around him. He was still breathing through his regulator. After roughly half a minute the whale surfaced, shook its head and threw him out, and his crewmate Josiah Mayo pulled him back aboard. He left hospital the same afternoon, badly bruised but with no broken bones. Whale scientists called it an accident: a feeding humpback that did not see him, and whose throat is far too narrow to swallow a person. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story.

source_notes: Date, place, name, age: Friday 11 June 2021, off Provincetown, Cape Cod; Michael Packard, 56, commercial lobster diver (AP via WBUR, NPR, NBC News). Depth: 'about 45 feet' (AP, NPR, NBC, Smithsonian, Live Science). What he felt: a 'huge bump' and 'everything went dark' (AP, NPR, Live Science); he compared it to a truck hitting him (NBC, Smithsonian), which the script paraphrases as 'hits him like a truck'. He first thought it was a shark, then noticed there were no teeth (all five). The slate's working title said 'swallowed'; he was held in the whale's mouth and never swallowed, so the title, script and graphics say 'mouth' and the case wall states SWALLOWED: NO. Breathing: AP, NPR, Smithsonian and Live Science say he kept breathing through his scuba regulator; NBC adds that he struggled to find it inside the mouth; the script says 'still breathing from his tank'. Time inside: 'about 30 seconds' (AP, Live Science), '30 to 40 seconds' by his own estimate (NPR, NBC, Smithsonian); the script says 'about thirty seconds'. He thought of his wife and sons (AP, NPR, Live Science; the sons' ages differ between NBC and Live Science, so no ages are given). The whale surfaced, shook its head and threw him out (all five); crewmate Josiah Mayo saw it and got him aboard (NPR, Smithsonian; NPR adds that a nearby charter captain helped, which the Short leaves out). Injuries: his sister first reported a broken leg, which he corrected (AP); he wrote that he was 'very bruised up but have no broken bones' (NPR); NBC, Smithsonian and Live Science also report a dislocated knee, which the script does not assert. He left Cape Cod Hospital that afternoon, limping (NPR) and was home that afternoon (NBC). Why: whale scientists quoted by AP, NPR and NBC (Charles 'Stormy' Mayo and Jooke Robbins of the Center for Coastal Studies, Iain Kerr of Ocean Alliance) called it an accident during feeding, probably on sand lance, and said a humpback could not swallow a person because its throat is too narrow (NPR; Live Science gives the general figure). Dramatised, not reported: the look of the boat, the pier and the hospital room, the crewman's clothes, the lobster under the ledge, the exact way the whale approached, the family photograph (drawn as three plain silhouettes), the breach beside the boat (sources say only that the whale surfaced), and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone. The slate's note about an earlier plane crash is true (Smithsonian) but not used.

quality_gate.method: 3D contact sheet reviewed in four rounds (the last at full frame size for eight key shots), composited stills (captions, HUD, overlays, inserts) in one, and a three-frames-per-shot strip from a full-length low-resolution rehearsal (216x384, 4 samples), which passed the automated gate locally: 39 shots, mean 1.11 s, longest 1.56 s, loudness -15.0 LUFS, voice 11.9 dB over the bed, host in 17/39 shots (44%), closest match to an earlier episode 0.78; caption pairs were measured against the frame width and the script reworded where a pair overflowed; the regulator's colour was changed after the rehearsal and not re-rendered; audio was measured, not listened to; the full-resolution render and final gate run in the cloud
